findings.title: Accidental git submodule added pointing at base commit
findings.body: This PR adds a new file `sentry-repo` as a git submodule (gitlink) pointing to commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a, which is the base commit of this very PR. This looks like an accidental artifact from running `git submodule add` against the repo itself rather than an intentional change. Merging this will add a broken/self-referential submodule entry to the repository, which can break clone/checkout tooling, CI, and confuse contributors. This should be removed before merge.

findings.title: Upsampling eligibility check uses outer `dataset` instead of the per-call `scoped_dataset`
findings.body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` is called with the closure variable `dataset` (computed once in `get()`), not the `scoped_dataset` parameter that is actually passed into this specific invocation. The dashboard-widget-split logic in `get_event_stats_factory` calls `_get_event_stats` multiple times with different `scoped_dataset` values (e.g. `discover` for `errors_only_query`, `discover` for `transactions_only_query`, or the original scoped dataset for the main query), but the upsampling eligibility/transform decision is always made against the single outer `dataset`. This means, for split queries, the eligibility check can use the wrong dataset (e.g. `metrics_performance` instead of `discover`), causing upsampling to incorrectly be skipped or applied for sub-queries whose actual dataset differs from the top-level dataset, producing silently wrong counts for error vs transaction split queries.

findings.title: Cache key built from Python's built-in hash(), risking collisions
findings.body: `cache_key = f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"` uses the built-in `hash()` over a tuple of project ids to build part of the cache key. Hash collisions (different project id sets producing the same hash value) are possible, which would make two different project-id sets share the same cache entry, causing one project group to be served a stale/incorrect eligibility decision cached for a completely different project set. A stable, collision-free key (e.g. joining sorted ids with a delimiter) should be used instead of `hash()`.

findings.title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but never called
findings.body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is intended to keep the 60-second eligibility cache in sync when the allowlist option changes, but nothing in this PR (or the shown diff) calls it from the option-update path. As a result the function is dead code and the cache will simply rely on its 60s TTL to expire, meaning there is no actual mechanism wired up to proactively invalidate on allowlist changes despite the function's docstring implying it should be invoked 'when the allowlist configuration changes'.

findings.title: Unused `organization` parameter in allowlist check suggests missing org scoping
findings.body: `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled(project_ids, organization)` accepts an `organization` argument but never references it in the function body; the allowlist check (`options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist")`) is purely global, keyed only on project ids. This is either dead code or indicates the allowlist was intended to be organization-scoped and that scoping was never implemented, which could allow unrelated organizations sharing a project id namespace collision or make per-org rollout of this option impossible even though the option name/semantics suggest per-org control.

findings.title: upsampled_count() only registered for discover dataset, but eligibility logic treats errors dataset as always eligible
findings.body: The new `upsampled_count` SnQL function is added only to `discover.py`'s `function_converter`. However, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` in `error_upsampling.py` unconditionally returns True for `dataset == errors` (the errors dataset module), meaning queries routed through `errors.py`'s dataset config will have their `count()` column rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count` by `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`. If the `errors` dataset's own function converter does not also define/inherit `upsampled_count`, those queries will fail at query-build time with an unknown-function error.

findings.title: Column transform only matches the exact literal 'count()'
findings.body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only transforms a column when, after lower-casing and stripping, it equals exactly `"count()"`. Any other common equivalent forms — e.g. `count() as total`, equations referencing `count()`, or whitespace inside the parentheses — are left untouched and silently fall through to regular `count()`, meaning the upsampling feature will not kick in for those forms even though the surrounding eligibility check indicated the query should be upsampled. This limited coverage is not documented as a known limitation and could cause inconsistent results depending on how the caller phrases the column.

findings.title: No tests cover the caching behavior that is central to the PR's performance claim
findings.body: The PR title advertises 'performance optimizations' via caching in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (60s TTL cache of allowlist eligibility), but none of the added tests exercise the caching path: there is no test for a cache hit returning a previously cached value, no test for cache expiry, and no test for `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. The existing tests only cover `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`, `_is_error_focused_query`, and `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` directly, bypassing the caching wrapper entirely.

findings.title: Broad exception swallowing hides malformed error_sampling context data
findings.body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the dict traversal and the float conversion in bare `except Exception: pass` blocks. Any malformed `contexts.error_sampling` structure (e.g. `contexts` present but not a dict, or a non-numeric `client_sample_rate`) will be silently ignored rather than surfaced, which can mask test setup bugs and make failures using this factory helper hard to diagnose since the event will just not get the expected `sample_rate` without any warning.
